entities.summary:
William of Saint-Amour was a key figure in thirteenth-century scholasticism, chiefly notable for his withering attacks on the friars. Born in France, Saint-Amour was a Dominican friar and theologian who rose to prominence through his critiques of the Dominican Order. His most influential work, the 'Quaestiones super libros decretalium,' offered a scathing critique of the friars' corruption and mismanagement.

Saint-Amour's attacks on the friars sparked a fierce debate within the Dominican Order, leading to a period of internal strife and power struggles. His criticisms also drew attention from other scholastic thinkers, who began to question the friars' role in the Church.

Despite his significant contributions to the development of scholasticism, Saint-Amour's legacy has been largely overshadowed by that of other prominent thinkers of the time. However, his work remains an important reminder of the complex and often fraught relationships between theologians, clergy, and the state during the Middle Ages.

The friars, who had once been the dominant force in Dominican life, were ultimately forced to adapt to the changing intellectual landscape. As the Dominican Order began to prioritize orthodoxy over pragmatism, Saint-Amour's critiques of the friars' excesses and corruption began to take on a new significance. Today, his work is seen as a crucial moment in the evolution of scholastic thought and the struggle for power within the Dominican Order.
